rationale: The entry's core identification — that 'the heart of the earth' in Matthew 12:40 denotes Jerusalem, the navel and center of the land — is carried by the cited texts better than the strongest specific alternative (the tomb/Sheol reading). Scripture nowhere calls a grave 'the heart of the earth,' but it does explicitly locate Jerusalem 'in the midst of the nations' (Ezek 5:5) and describes the regathered people dwelling at the tabbur ('navel') of the land (Ezek 38:12). The mirrored Hebrew idiom in Jonah's own prayer ('the heart of the seas,' Jonah 2:3) supplies an inner-biblical control: with the sea as peoples (Rev 17:15), the heart of the seas is the midst of the nations, and the heart of the earth/land is symmetrically the land's center — the city God set in the midst. Extra-biblical witnesses (Philo's 'heart of the whole earth,' the Sibylline 'navel and heart of the earth') confirm the phrase was a known title of Jerusalem in Jesus' world. The Jerusalem reading also resolves the 'three days and three nights' count (arrest night to third-day resurrection, Luke 24:21) that the tomb reading can satisfy only by treating the duration as loose idiom or relocating the crucifixion day — both larger unsupported steps. The tomb counter explains no supplied text that the Jerusalem core cannot accommodate: death, burial, and Sheol language all fall within the interval of Jerusalem's custody, and Jonah — alive and praying in the belly — is in any case a poor match for a corpse in a tomb. Every material assertion actually printed in the entry ('Jerusalem,' 'navel,' 'heart of the land') is supported by the printed references.
book_core_identification: 'The heart of the earth' (Matt 12:40) refers to Jerusalem — the city God set in the midst of the nations and land, its navel and center — rather than to the tomb or the underworld as such.
book_secondary_elaborations: Jerusalem is the 'navel' of the land, anchored in tabbur at Ezekiel 38:12 ('midst of the land').
Jerusalem is the 'heart' of the land, anchored in Ezekiel 5:5 ('I have set it in the midst of the nations').
chapter_only_objections: The claim that the three-days count begins at the arrest outside the gates (Jesus under Jerusalem's custody) even though the crucifixion and burial occurred outside the city wall requires the polity-custody argument, which is a chapter-level construction, not printed in the entry.
The identification of the great fish with Caesar/Rome as the devouring ruler is a chapter-level typological claim.

The scene-by-scene Jonah–Passion parallel table (Judas as Jonah's flight, the fare as the thirty pieces, the reeds as the crown of thorns, lots for garments, etc.) is chapter-level typology beyond the entry.
The reading of Nineveh's 'three days' journey' as three thousand years via 2 Peter 3:8 is a speculative chapter-level chronology.
The claim that the Ninevites 'shall rise' refers to literal resurrection (anastēsontai) joining the saints who judge the world is a chapter-level inference.
The dependence on sea = peoples (Rev 17:15) and ship = polity (Ezek 27) as fully 'defined symbols' is argued in other chapters and deferred to Part Six; the entry itself does not assert these.
strongest_counter_interpretation: 'The heart of the earth' means the tomb/grave and, by extension, Sheol/Hades — the interior of the earth where Jesus lay between death and resurrection. On this reading the Hebrew idiom lev-yammim ('heart of the seas,' Ezek 27:4; Jonah 2:3) denotes depth and interiority, not a geographic capital, so 'heart of the earth' naturally means down inside the earth; the Jonah parallel (belly of the fish, 'belly of Sheol,' Jonah 2:2) and Acts 2:27/Ps 16:10 ('not leave my soul in hell... nor see corruption') then point to burial and the realm of the dead.
counter_core_identification: The tomb/grave and Sheol — the physical or spiritual interior of the earth where the dead Christ lay before rising.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that 'the heart of the earth' names Jerusalem at all: it holds that the phrase locates Jesus beneath the earth's surface (grave/Sheol), not within a city at the land's center. Both identifications cannot be true as the primary referent of the same phrase.
counter_case: The lev-X idiom ('heart of the seas,' Ezek 27:4, 26; Ps 46:2) denotes the deep interior of a domain, so 'heart of the earth' most naturally means deep within the earth — the grave.
Jonah's prayer explicitly says he cried 'out of the belly of Sheol' (Jonah 2:2), tying the fish's belly to the realm of the dead, which matches a dead and buried Christ.
Acts 2:27/Ps 16:10 ('not suffer thine Holy One to see corruption') and the burial narratives (Matt 27:57-60) supply an obvious referent: the tomb.
The near-universal interpretive tradition takes the phrase as burial/descent, and 'three days and three nights' can be treated as inclusive Jewish day-count idiom (cf. Esther 4:16 with 5:1).
book_explanatory_advantages: Ezekiel 5:5 explicitly names Jerusalem as set 'in the midst of the nations,' and Ezekiel 38:12's tabbur ('navel of the land') gives the entry's exact vocabulary; no Scripture ever calls a grave 'the heart of the earth.'

The mirrored phrase in the very sign Jesus cites — Jonah in 'the heart of the seas' — was not the fish's belly alone but the midst of the raging peoples, and with sea = peoples (Rev 17:15) the symmetry reads heart of the earth/land = midst of the nations = Jerusalem.

Contemporary usage (Philo: 'heart of the whole earth'; Sibylline Oracles: 'the navel and heart of the earth'; Greek Ezekiel variants) shows the phrase was a recognized title of Jerusalem in Jesus' linguistic world.

The Jerusalem reading yields an exact three-days-and-three-nights count from the night arrest to the third-day resurrection (Luke 24:21), where the tomb reading must either dilute the duration into idiom or move the crucifixion day.

Jonah in the fish is alive and praying (Jonah 2:1), 'as good as dead' but not a corpse — a better match for Jesus held in the city's hostile custody through trial, death, and burial than for a body lying inert in a tomb.
counter_explanatory_advantages: It fits the plain depth-sense of the lev-yammim idiom without invoking the symbolic equation sea = peoples.
It connects directly to Jonah 2:2 ('belly of Sheol') and Acts 2:27, and to the burial narratives, without any typological machinery.
It matches the overwhelming interpretive tradition, so it demands no revision of the received chronology framework beyond treating the day-count as idiom.
decisive_sources: Ezekiel 5:5 — 'This is Jerusalem: I have set it in the midst of the nations,' Scripture's own explicit location of the land's heart.
Ezekiel 38:12 — tabbur, 'the navel of the land,' supplying the entry's exact 'navel' vocabulary.
Jonah 2:3 (bilvav yammim, 'heart of the seas') as the mirrored phrase within the very sign Matthew 12:40 invokes.
Matthew 12:40 read against Luke 24:21 — the exact three-days-and-three-nights count that the Jerusalem reading satisfies and the Friday-burial tomb reading cannot without extra steps.
Philo and the Sibylline Oracles as contemporary attestation that 'heart/navel of the earth' named Jerusalem.
unresolved_objections: The lev-yammim idiom elsewhere plainly denotes depth within the sea (Ezek 27:4, 26), so a non-symbolic reader could take 'heart of the earth' as sheer interiority; the book's rebuttal depends on the sea = peoples symbol established primarily outside the supplied excerpts.

Jesus' crucifixion and burial outside the city wall strains a strictly geographic 'in Jerusalem' and is resolved only by the chapter's custody/polity argument, which is out of scope for the entry itself.
